I'm a 60-year-old farmer in Quzhou with 40 years on these fields and a high-school education. Six mu isn't much land, but with six people under my roof, family labor is the one thing I have in abundance. Cash is tight — I can't afford to gamble on new varieties or push fertilizer rates to the extension maximum. My strategy this year is to lean on the cabbage-maize-cabbage backbone for stable bulk income, while using small plots of chili, kidney bean, and spinach to squeeze out extra margin where the market rewards labor.

**Spring cabbage (1.5 mu):** I'll plant in late February, using hybrid seed I buy fresh — about 55 yuan per mu. I've seen too many disease problems with saved cabbage seed. Based on last year's performance and the soil texture on my eastern plot, I'm targeting 18 kg N per mu, 8 kg P₂O₅, and 10 kg K₂O. I'll put down a 15-15-15 compound as basal at roughly 25 kg per mu, then topdress with urea at rosette stage. Four irrigations from the well: transplanting, rosette, heading, and one backup if April stays dry. The well water is metered now, so each irrigation costs me about 20–25 yuan per mu. I'll spray herbicide once before transplanting and insecticide twice for cabbage worms. Yield should be around 1,400 kg per mu if the spring weather cooperates.

**Summer maize (1.5 mu):** This goes in around June 10th on the plot that carried spring cabbage, after I get the residue cleared and the land rotavated. I'm using the same hybrid as the last three years — it doesn't top the yield contests, but it gives me a reliable 500 kg per mu with two irrigations and minimal fuss. I'll apply compound fertilizer at sowing for about 12 kg N per mu, then one urea side-dress at jointing. One herbicide application at pre-emergence is enough; insect pressure on maize has been light. I hire my neighbor's no-till planter for 30 yuan per mu because my old machine skips seeds, but harvest is all family labor with the combine.

**Fall cabbage (1.5 mu):** I transplant in mid-August on the northern plot. This is my insurance crop — if chili prices collapse, I can usually move fall cabbage at decent prices before the New Year. Same fertilizer approach as spring, maybe slightly less nitrogen since temperatures drop during heading. I'll irrigate four times. Aphids are the main worry in autumn, so I'll keep insecticide on hand.

**Chili (1.0 mu):** This is where my labor goes. I'll transplant in early May. Chili seed is expensive — around 120 yuan per mu for the hybrid I use — but the return per mu is the highest on my farm. I'm budgeting 20 kg N per mu, split across basal and two side-dresses during flowering and fruit set. Five irrigations, because chili stress at flowering ruins the crop. Pesticide is the real cost here: I'll rotate insecticide and fungicide every 10 to 14 days through July and August. Aphids, thrips, and anthracnose are constant threats. I expect about 2,500 kg per mu of fresh chili if the monsoon doesn't flood the flowers.

**Kidney bean (0.5 mu):** I'll sow in early May on the small plot near the house, mostly for family eating with surplus sold at village market. Beans fix some nitrogen, so I keep N modest at about 10 kg per mu, but I push phosphorus and potassium for pod set. I'll put up simple bamboo stakes — no trellis wire, too expensive. Five irrigations and weekly insecticide sprays during pod fill. Labor is heavy because I hand-pick every three days during peak season.

**Spinach (0.5 mu):** After the beans finish in late September, I'll quickly turn that plot and sow spinach by October 1st. It's a 70-day crop that gives me cash right before Spring Festival. One basal application of compound at about 12 kg N per mu, two irrigations, and minimal pest pressure. The seed costs about 80 yuan per mu.

On labor, my family covers almost everything. The only hired cost is maize sowing. With six people, we can manage the intense picking schedules for chili and beans without hiring day laborers at 120 yuan a day. Total input cash outlay this season will be about 3,850 yuan, which is most of my savings. I'm not experimenting — consistency feeds my family.
